rv.q: If the premise of Head Over Heels sounds a little nutso, that’s because the show is a lot nutso, in the most delightfully daffy, exuberantly heart-open way.
"Head Over Heels" is a delightfully entertaining romp, an impressive display of theatrical creativity that leaves you in awe of any mind capable of dreaming it up.
To enjoy Head Over Heels, which offers quite a lot to enjoy, it is probably best to kick up your heels and put your head on hold.
This appears to be written around weak songs trying to take advantage of ABBA’s Mama Mia.

The amalgam is so brazen as to be immediately disarming: it would take a truly bad sport not to get on board with ersatz Elizabethan verse (“Please ventilate the belfry of thy mind”) side by side with eighties earworms like “Our Lips Are Sealed,” delivered with equal gusto by a game cast.
I'm afraid that the stylistic dissonance between the show's book and its songs ultimately proves to be an insurmountable problem.
Head Over Heels just strikes as winking and self-satisfied, occasionally amusing, occasionally cloying.
This jukebox experiment doesn't succeed, but by the time 'Mad About You' is reprised at the end, some genuine new wave Elizabethan feeling sneaks through.

But “Head Over Heels,” which is so anxious to please as to be overplayed, is too arch to drive real suspense (the obstacles to happiness are too easily overcome) and not detailed enough in how it explores this music to allow you to feel a sufficiently organic connection.
“Head Over Heels” lacks the courage of its contradictions.
But despite the ample professionalism on display, the show comes across as painfully strained rather than pleasurably antic.
But the show never recovers from the pervasive feeling of exhaustion.
This indulgent show is wackier than it is fun, and elicits more “huh?” than “ha”.

Unfortunately, the play isn’t any good, though that won’t matter, since it fulfills the first condition of success on Broadway: It tells the members of the audience what they want to hear, and nothing else.
This wonderful, exuberant musical enjoins us to unseal our lips and fight for just that.
Shrewd, funny, sexy, and with a glorious beat, Head Over Heels will have you flipping for joy.
Since not all of us can afford a summer getaway, a trip to “Head Over Heels” may be the brief but satisfying vacation we all need.
For two hours and 15 minutes, it’s enough to pull the world back into sync.
You'll be head over heels by the time the curtain falls.

Speaking of beats: As soon as the curtain goes up, you’ll hear the unmistakable driving drum riff of “We Got the Beat,” one of the band’s first (and best) singles, here transformed into a rousing full-company production number packed with exhaustingly good choreography by Spencer Liff.
Head Over Heels lacks the courage of its contradictions.
Bottom line: if you think you've got the beat, and you are ready for some good old "romp and roll," then by all means head on out to Head Over Heels where both are in ample supply.
Under Michael Mayer’s fast-paced direction, Head Over Heels starts badly and busily but eventually slows down to a delightful Elizabethan parody on love and gender.
Head Over Heels is a witty endorsement of love and acceptance in all its contemporary forms, especially gay/queer/gender-fluid.
On paper, Head Over Heels may not be to everyone's taste (including this reviewer), but it certainly achieves its goal of providing glossy, energetic fun.
The result is one of the most elaborately staged jukebox musicals you're likely to ever have seen.
What’s spoken on stage is often amusing and sometimes hilarious.

The convoluted story revolves around a king and queen, their two daughters and a shepherd love interest. Their lives do indeed turn head over heels as King Bacilius visits the Oracle Pythio who portends a series of calamitous events. It gets awfully complicated and audiences may tune out before it's all resolved.
Head over Heels broadly succeeds because of the inclusivity of its non-binary message.
Also, the plot wears thin over the musical’s two hours and 15 minutes, with dramatic breakthroughs explained instead of felt.
The most surprising thing, perhaps, is that after all is said and done, this purposely low-brow, far-from-subtle propaganda statement for sexual equality turns out to be a wittily wicked romp.
But where “Spring Awakening” worked brilliantly well, “Head Over Heels” misfires.
It all works and it’s all fabulous; habemus percussio.
You’ll have a joyful night at Head Over Heels, Twelfth Night, or Fiddler, but This Ain’t No Disco ain’t worth your time.
It's also an infectiously entertaining, french-tipped fist pump for the resistance.
Love and desire triumphs over power plays and deceit, giving us all a joyous slice of 80’s girl band heaven that truly is a place on Broadway’s Earth.
An exuberant, raucous and joyous musical

"The show is ground-breaking. It’s about sexual identity and the struggles that come along with it...It’s about freedom. Liberation. Acceptance. And the theme weaves in and out of the story effortlessly, all the way to the dancers and choreography...The songs are wonderful, as you’d expect them to be, and they are well sung by a skilled cast.
Get past that (and I did) and you will enjoy a fizzy, lusty tale of love, desire, freedom and tolerance.

The cast is hardworking and talented, especially the amazing Bonnie Milligan as the more narcissistic of the two daughters and the Peter Scolari-ish Andrew Durand as the lead drag queen, who breaks fourth walls and romantic barriers.

A lot of theatrical smarts are on view in Head Over Heels, but this new jukebox Broadway musical also has a tendency to wallow in some low-grade smirking, even as it offers a celebration of love in general, both hetero and homo.
This musical is a bit messy, but it's fun and it is doing some very important work for representation and visibility on Broadway.
The result is a messy, uneven production that fails to engage on any level.
Against all odds, it mostly works.
The show grows on you if you simply go along with it and accept it for nothing other than the mindless, splashy entertainment it is.
If you enjoy a silly farce with music but which can be confusing, you will enjoy this musical.
For everyone else, they’ll have to decide for themselves if they should go-go see it.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Go-Go's/Elizabethan mash-up, with most finding it a goofy, energetic romp that champions inclusivity, though some dismiss the odd pairing as too silly and the transitions between period dialogue and '80s pop jarring.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored 1903 gem — one of the most gorgeous small theaters on Broadway. The 2017 renovation delivered some of the widest and most comfortable seats in the Theater District, with excellent sightlines from the intimate 970-seat house.

acc.note: Elevator to Dress Circle. No elevator to Balcony. Assisted listening devices at coat check.
